messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

José, a 22-year-old Latin American man and HVAC technician, had experienced a traumatic event that continues to haunt him. One day at work, while he was on a routine job installing an air conditioning unit in a high-rise building, a mishap occurred. He accidentally knocked the ladder loose, causing his coworker, Luis, to fall from the third floor. The sound of the impact and Luis’s screams were seared into José's memory. Though Luis survived with severe injuries, José was overwhelmed by guilt and self-recrimination. José had come to believe that he could no longer trust his own body, which felt unreliable in moments when his physical reactions seemed out of his control. The event also left him feeling unrecognizable to himself; the person who used to be confident and competent now found it difficult to look at his reflection without seeing a stranger. He harbored deep feelings of guilt for not doing more to prevent the accident, despite being certain that he had no way to stop what happened. These negative appraisals led José to engage in maladaptive strategies such as avoiding anniversaries connected to the event and any other potential stressors. This avoidance became a habit, and it reinforced his belief that he could not trust himself or his body. He felt compelled to overanalyze every detail of the accident, trying desperately to make sense of how something so terrible could have happened under his watch. The memory of Luis falling had become alien to him; it felt like it belonged to someone else rather than to himself. When he thought about the event, he could smell the pungent scent of oil and metal from the air conditioning unit, which only intensified his sense that something dangerous was looming. This olfactory recall often triggered strong physical reactions, such as a racing heart and sweating palms, especially in moments of unusual silence. These memories began to force their way into his mind at unexpected times, leading José to feel an ever-present threat. He developed the belief that he could only feel safe within a very limited number of places, primarily his home or familiar environments. This sense of threat was further exacerbated by any reminders of the event, such as working on ladders or hearing similar metallic sounds. Over time, this cycle tightened. José’s overanalyzing and avoidance behaviors reinforced his negative appraisals, creating a self-reinforcing loop that kept him in a constant state of hypervigilance and anxiety. He found it increasingly difficult to concentrate at work, which led to more stress and further avoidance behaviors. His relationships suffered as well; he pushed away friends and coworkers who tried to engage with him, fearing they might see the unrecognizable self he now perceived. José’s current state was marked by a profound sense of isolation and guilt. He had finally sought help after realizing that his attempts at coping were only making things worse. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never be able to forgive himself for what happened, and the constant worry that something equally dangerous might happen again. Despite this, he was hopeful that with support, he could find a way to reclaim control over his life and begin to trust himself once more.
